## Gastronomic tours in Ecuador: what to choose

**There are two very different ways to discover Ecuador's flavors: mainland cacao and creative cuisine on a sea voyage.** Both itineraries combine food experiences with substantial sightseeing. If you want a dedicated culinary vacation, remember that a gastronomic theme does not mean every day includes markets, tastings or workshops.

Our catalog currently includes {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}}. Each route has its own main purpose, so judge its culinary component by the actual daily program and specified services.

| Program | Gastronomic focus |
|---|---|
| [New Year in Ecuador](/ecuador/tour/complete-ecuador-new-year/) | Cacao plantation and chocolate |
| [Aqua Mare cruise](/ecuador/tour/galapagos-luxury-yacht-cruise-8-days/) | Seafood and Nikkei cuisine |

Both journeys take place in Ecuador, but their geographies barely overlap. The first travels through the Andes to Guayaquil before flying to the islands; the second involves several days aboard a yacht exploring the Galápagos archipelago.

## Cacao and chocolate: a culinary day between Cuenca and Guayaquil

Ecuador is known for fino de aroma cacao, aromatic varieties linked to local traditions of growing and processing cacao. The crop is important to national history too: farms, trade and bean processing shaped life in the coastal provinces. An ordinary chocolate bar shows only the finished product. Visiting a plantation reveals what the fruit looks like, what happens to the beans before roasting and why fermentation affects taste.

On the [Ecuador New Year tour](/ecuador/tour/complete-ecuador-new-year/), the culinary experience is scheduled for January 5, 2027. After [Cuenca](/ecuador/place/cuenca/), the group travels via [Cajas National Park](/ecuador/place/cajas-national-park/) toward [Guayaquil](/ecuador/place/guayaquil/). The separate [“Cajas and Cacao Plantation” excursion](/ecuador/cajas-national-park/cajas-and-cacao-workshop/) combines high-altitude lakes with an introduction to chocolate. Breakfast and lunch are listed for the day.

The contrast is fascinating: cool Andean highlands in the morning, followed by a journey into another ecological zone to learn about a tropical crop. But this is **one gastronomic day on a longer trip**, not a multi-day chocolatier course. If cacao is your principal goal, check the content of the [plantation excursion](/ecuador/cajas-national-park/cajas-and-cacao-workshop/) rather than expecting additional tastings that do not appear in the itinerary.

The tour has a specific calendar: a group departure from December 30, 2026 to January 9, 2027. Besides cacao, it includes [Quito and Cotopaxi](/ecuador/place/quito-and-cotopaxi-volcano/), [Cuenca](/ecuador/place/cuenca/), Andean waterfalls and the [Galápagos Islands](/ecuador/place/galapagos-islands/). The mainland guide speaks Russian and the Galápagos guide speaks English.

## Galápagos Islands: seafood and Nikkei cuisine aboard a yacht

During the [eight-day Aqua Mare cruise](/ecuador/tour/galapagos-luxury-yacht-cruise-8-days/), gastronomy forms part of onboard life. The program mentions fresh fish and seafood, Ecuadorian dishes with Andean influences and Nikkei cuisine, which combines Japanese cooking techniques with South American ingredients and flavors. Consulting chef Pedro Miguel Schiaffino developed the yacht's menu.

This is a different food experience from a farm visit: the meals accompany evenings after island landings and outings at sea. Advertised dishes include shrimp ceviche, tuna crudo, fish, potato llapingachos and dishes with local seafood. According to the program, onboard meals, selected premium wines and beer are included. These terms apply to **this cruise**, not automatically to all travel in Ecuador.

The main reason to choose the [yacht itinerary](/ecuador/tour/galapagos-luxury-yacht-cruise-8-days/) is nevertheless the islands, volcanic shores and wildlife. The route covers [Santa Cruz](/ecuador/place/santa-cruz-island/), [Floreana](/ecuador/place/floreana-island/), [Isabela](/ecuador/place/isabela-island/) and other sites. Certain days feature wildlife watching, snorkeling and guided walks. Choose this cruise for the combination of these landings and thoughtfully planned meals, not an implied promise of daily cooking workshops.

## What about Ecuadorian wineries, coffee and separate tastings?

The general “Food and Wine” category covers different offerings throughout Latin America. **Neither current Ecuadorian itinerary advertises a winery visit.** Calling this selection an Ecuadorian wine tour would be misleading.

Outside the particular tours, the country has much more to taste. Ecuadorian tourism materials describe cacao estates, highland coffee in Loja and varied coastal and Andean cuisines. Those traditions do not mean that the [mainland Ecuador tour](/ecuador/tour/complete-ecuador-new-year/) includes a coffee estate or that the [Galápagos cruise](/ecuador/tour/galapagos-luxury-yacht-cruise-8-days/) includes a separate chocolate lesson.

If you primarily want wineries and several days of tastings, explore the [general gastronomic travel selection](/interests/food-and-wine/tours/) and compare wine routes in other countries. To learn about Ecuadorian traditions beyond a specific product, read the [Ecuador guide](/ecuador/).

## Choosing by time and content

Start with how much time you want to devote to the main food experience. A single cacao day fits into a longer New Year trip through the Andes, while restaurant-quality cuisine on a cruise accompanies several island days. Travelers hoping to meet producers and study food preparation have different expectations from those who enjoy excellent dining on vacation.

**Check three details in the chosen program:** whether production visits or simply meals are included; which dishes, drinks and tastings are covered; and whether there is free time for independent restaurants. The [New Year tour](/ecuador/tour/complete-ecuador-new-year/) has fixed dates and a group format. For the [Aqua Mare cruise](/ecuador/tour/galapagos-luxury-yacht-cruise-8-days/), examine the island sequence, accommodation arrangements and onboard meals.

Travel from the Andes to the coast involves major changes of altitude and climate. A flight is necessary between the mainland and the [Galápagos](/ecuador/place/galapagos-islands/). An additional farm, restaurant or culinary activity therefore constitutes an itinerary change, not a service automatically included.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is there a ready-made Ecuadorian tour that visits a cacao plantation?

Yes. The [“Complete Ecuador at New Year” program](/ecuador/tour/complete-ecuador-new-year/) includes a separate [excursion through Cajas to a cacao plantation](/ecuador/cajas-national-park/cajas-and-cacao-workshop/). It occupies part of a larger journey across the Andes and islands.

### Can I travel to Ecuador specifically for wine tasting?

Our thematic selection does not advertise Ecuadorian winery visits. If wine is the main purpose, choose an itinerary explicitly listing wineries and tastings; compare destinations in the [overall gastronomic tour catalog](/interests/food-and-wine/tours/).

### What counts as gastronomy on a Galápagos cruise?

The [Aqua Mare cruise](/ecuador/tour/galapagos-luxury-yacht-cruise-8-days/) offers a creative Nikkei menu, local fish, seafood and included onboard meals. The principal excursion program focuses on the islands and their wildlife.

### Can a gastronomic trip suit someone who does not drink alcohol?

Cacao and chocolate experiences are independent of wine. On the [yacht cruise](/ecuador/tour/galapagos-luxury-yacht-cruise-8-days/), check the menu and included drinks: having wine in the package does not require a guest to consume it.

### Can gastronomy be combined with Ecuadorian nature?

Both current options do so. The [mainland New Year route](/ecuador/tour/complete-ecuador-new-year/) connects cacao with the Andes and the [Galápagos](/ecuador/place/galapagos-islands/), while the [eight-day cruise](/ecuador/tour/galapagos-luxury-yacht-cruise-8-days/) pairs onboard cuisine with landings and wildlife observation.

## How to choose a gastronomic tour from current programs

Our catalog features {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}}. It includes **specialized wine and coffee itineraries**, along with broader journeys where food takes several days among city excursions, nature and leisure. Start with your specific goal: visiting several wineries, learning how coffee travels from berry to cup, trying regional dishes or adding gastronomic stops to a larger trip.

Compare **the full days devoted to the main theme**. Winery visits may be central to one nine-day program, while another nine-day itinerary has just one coffee-farm stop. Both have their merits, but serve different purposes.

Look at what each visit involves. A “winery visit” may include vineyards, production, tasting and lunch, or just some of those activities. A coffee excursion may explore the estate's history or take you through growing, drying, roasting and brewing. The specific offering is described in each itinerary.

For quick comparisons, select a country and open several itineraries of similar duration. The country selections for [Argentina](/interests/food-and-wine/tours/argentina/), [Brazil](/interests/food-and-wine/tours/brazil/), [Colombia](/interests/food-and-wine/tours/colombia/) and [Uruguay](/interests/food-and-wine/tours/uruguay/) help narrow the search.

## Wine tours: Mendoza, Chile or Uruguay

If wine is your main reason to travel, first compare two Argentine routes. The [7-day “Argentina for Lovers of Wine, Cuisine and the Good Life”](/argentina/tour/argentina-food-fine-living/) combines [Buenos Aires](/argentina/place/buenos-aires/) with [Mendoza](/argentina/place/mendoza/). The capital offers architecture, tango and gaucho traditions, while the food-and-wine part continues among Andean vineyards. There is a traditional estancia lunch and an introduction to Argentine cuisine. One day in Mendoza is left for optional activities, so not every hour should be treated as a mandatory tasting.

The [nine-day Argentina–Chile wine tour](/multi-country/tour/chile-argentina-mendoza-wine-9-days/) covers Buenos Aires, Mendoza and Santiago de Chile. In the [Uco Valley](/argentina/place/uco-valley/), the group visits three wineries with a specialist guide, learns about production, tastes wines and lunches at one winery. In Chile, the route includes [Concha y Toro](/chile/place/concha-y-toro/) and its vineyards. This is for people interested in two winemaking countries who are willing to spend part of their vacation on an international transfer.

For a closer look at individual wine days, see the [Mendoza wineries excursion](/argentina/mendoza/mendoza-wineries-wine-tasting/), the [Luján de Cuyo trip with three tastings and lunch](/argentina/mendoza/argentina-lujan-three-wineries-lunch/), or the [Maipo Valley wine tour](/chile/maipo-valley/maipo-valley-wine-tour/). Each is a separate excursion product; its presence on the website does not automatically include it in a multi-day tour.

Uruguay has another approach. The [four-day “Wine and Old Believer Traditions” tour](/uruguay/tour/uruguay-wine-old-believer-traditions/) visits Montevideo, [Spinoglio Winery](/uruguay/place/spinoglio-winery/), [San Javier](/uruguay/place/san-javier/) and Colonia del Sacramento. A winery visit here accompanies history and encounters with local communities. The [six-day “Best of Uruguay” tour](/uruguay/tour/best-of-uruguay-five-star-tour/) connects Montevideo with Punta del Este and lists two wineries and food experiences. Choose a shorter history-and-wine journey or a longer coastal holiday according to your goal.

| Itinerary | What to compare |
|---|---|
| [Argentina, 7 days](/argentina/tour/argentina-food-fine-living/) | Wine, cuisine and the capital |
| [Argentina + Chile, 9 days](/multi-country/tour/chile-argentina-mendoza-wine-9-days/) | Uco Valley and Concha y Toro |
| [Uruguay, 4 days](/uruguay/tour/uruguay-wine-old-believer-traditions/) | Winery and history |
| [Uruguay, 6 days](/uruguay/tour/best-of-uruguay-five-star-tour/) | Two wineries and the ocean |

The point is to decide how much time you want for wine. Numbers of visits, distances, tastings, lunches and free hours matter more than the generic label “wine tour.”

## Coffee journeys: production or plantation history

**Coffee tours in Colombia and Brazil tell different sides of the same story.** Colombian routes can focus on present-day farms and processing methods; Brazilian trips may explore historic fazendas, old machinery and the place of coffee estates in national history.

The [six-day “Colombia Coffee” trip](/colombia/tour/colombia-coffee/) visits Bogotá, Zipaquirá, [Pereira](/colombia/place/pereira/), [Salento](/colombia/place/salento/) and Cocora Valley. A coffee-farm tour covers cultivation, harvesting, drying, grinding and roasting, ending in a tasting. This is for travelers who want to see how coffee is produced but still leave time for the capital and nature.

The [ten-day Bogotá, Medellín and Cartagena tour with coffee](/colombia/tour/colombia-bogota-medellin-cartagena-coffee-10-days/) has a different focus. The early days include a visit to [Hacienda Coloma](/colombia/place/hacienda-coloma/), after which the route moves through other cities. If coffee production is your main goal, assess how long the farm visit actually lasts. To see several major cities as well, the broader route can be convenient.

The separate [nine-day Bogotá, Pereira and Cartagena tour](/colombia/tour/colombia-bogota-eje-cafetero-cartagena-9-days/) includes [Hacienda Venecia](/colombia/place/hacienda-venecia/) in the coffee region. Here you learn the bean's journey from plantation to cup, but the itinerary also focuses on urban history and landscapes. For more specialized experiences, there are standalone [coffee-farm tours from Pereira](/colombia/pereira/pereira-coffee-farm-tour/) and [to El Ocaso near Salento](/colombia/salento/el-ocaso-coffee-farm-tour/). Check each visit's terms: a separate excursion and the multi-day package need not have the same inclusions.

In Brazil, consider the [eight-day coffee tour including Rio and Iguazú](/brazil/tour/brazil-coffee-tour-8-days/). It connects classic Rio sightseeing and the waterfalls with a day at a historic coffee fazenda: manor house, outbuildings, equipment and tasting. A [nine-day private Brazil coffee tour](/brazil/tour/brazil-private-coffee-tour/) adds the historic [Coffee Valley of Rio de Janeiro state](/brazil/place/coffee-valley-rio-de-janeiro/) and Visconde de Mauá. It is an introduction to coffee heritage and several natural regions, not a trip exclusively devoted to modern coffee processing.

The same historic theme can be explored on a separate [tour of the coffee barons' estates](/brazil/excursion/coffee-baron-estates-tour/). Choose between a single day and a longer itinerary according to whether one fazenda visit suffices or you also want several regions of Brazil.

## Gastronomic Mexico and journeys where cuisine accompanies travel

Food is one of the central themes of the [nine-day Mexico gastronomic tour](/mexico/tour/mexico-gourmet-discovery-2024/). Its program explores San Juan and Medellín markets, taquerías and local cuisine, including tacos and mezcal. It also takes in historic districts of Mexico City, Xochimilco, Teotihuacán and Yucatán landmarks. This suits a traveler who wants to understand food alongside cities, history and everyday life.

Mexican cuisine is famous for varied regional methods and ingredients; its culinary traditions are listed by UNESCO as intangible heritage. But even on a food-centered trip, **a market visit, a mezcal tasting and a full cooking workshop are different services**. Do not presume a cooking lesson is included unless it is expressly listed in a day's program or among paid add-ons.

For the cuisine of one region, explore [Oaxaca](/mexico/place/oaxaca/) and its [cultural city excursions](/mexico/oaxaca/oaxaca-walking-tour/). Add them separately if logistics genuinely permit. Mentioning Oaxaca here does not mean it is part of the nine-day food program.

Other itineraries make food **a highlight within a different primary theme**. For example, the [six-day Peru journey on the Belmond Hiram Bingham train](/peru/tour/peru-belmond-hiram-bingham-machu-picchu/) focuses on Lima, Cusco, the Sacred Valley and Machu Picchu. The train program describes a dining car, brunch and a gourmet dinner. It is a culinary experience that complements a cultural itinerary without converting every day into a food excursion.

## Reading the program: tastings, transfers and included services

Before comparing prices, open the daily schedules and record four facts: how many wineries or farms you actually visit, whether tasting is included, where lunches are scheduled and how much time travel takes. **One tasting and a full day at multiple estates provide different levels of experience.**

| What to check | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Farm visits | Time spent on the main theme |
| Tastings | Contents of the paid visit |
| Lunches | Where and whose expense |
| Transfers | Time between locations |
| Free days | Possibility of adding a visit |

On the [nine-day Argentina–Chile wine journey](/multi-country/tour/chile-argentina-mendoza-wine-9-days/), lunch is provided at a Uco Valley winery, while lunch during the Concha y Toro excursion is listed as a separately paid option. These distinctions affect the budget and must not be generalized from one winery visit to the rest.

Prices can be per person or per group, and included services differ even between similar routes. Check currency, accommodation category, meals, tickets, guides, local and international flights. A program that features tastings does not necessarily pay for every drink and restaurant bill.

Consider **how many additional days the geography itself requires**. Within [Mendoza](/argentina/place/mendoza/), wineries can be visited in one region; combining Argentina and Chile adds international travel. Colombia's Bogotá–Pereira–Cartagena route lets you experience several regions but reduces the number of full farm days. In Uruguay, a winery trip from Montevideo can fit into a shorter stay.

For one wine day within an established trip, see [private tastings in Luján de Cuyo](/argentina/lujan-de-cuyo/lujan-de-cuyo-winery-tasting/) or [Montevideo with a wine tasting](/uruguay/montevideo/montevideo-city-winery-tour/). These show possible additions, not a guarantee they fit particular dates, transfers and plans.

## Seasons: when harvest matters and when it does not

For tastings of mature wines, **traveling during harvest is not necessary**. Wineries may receive guests in other seasons, and each estate sets its own tour content. If you want to watch grapes being harvested, confirm the dates for the specific vineyard.

Mendoza's Vendimia celebrations traditionally fall in February and March. Official Argentine tourism materials distinguish Uco Valley, Luján de Cuyo and Maipú as winemaking areas. The festival, a tasting and taking part in grape harvesting are different activities, however; the selected tour does not automatically include the event. Check the scheduled wine days rather than relying on a vague “wine season.”

Coffee timing depends even more on country and region. Colombia's highland farms differ from Brazil's historic fazendas in climate and purpose. **Picking coffee berries is only one possible activity**. Explanations of varieties, drying, roasting and tasting remain worthwhile outside harvest. Traditions and settlement architecture are an important part of Colombia's coffee cultural landscape.

In Mexico, establish your preferred format first: markets and restaurants, a specific regional trip, a festival or a cooking lesson. Opening schedules, special tastings and events need to be checked for your travel dates. A food-and-wine category tag cannot replace that check.

## Frequently asked questions about choosing gastronomic tours

### How long should a wine tour of Argentina be?

To combine the capital with Mendoza, start with a [seven-day trip](/argentina/tour/argentina-food-fine-living/). To visit wineries in both Argentina and Chile, a [nine-day itinerary](/multi-country/tour/chile-argentina-mendoza-wine-9-days/) is available. Choose according to the number of winery visits and how comfortable you are with added transfers.

### Colombia or Brazil for my first coffee tour?

If you primarily want to see bean processing at a working farm, compare the [six-day Colombia coffee tour](/colombia/tour/colombia-coffee/) with other Pereira-region journeys. If historic fazendas, old estates and a combination with Rio and Iguazú attract you, consider the [eight-day Brazil program](/brazil/tour/brazil-coffee-tour-8-days/).

### Are tastings and lunches included?

That depends on the selected tour. Even on the same [nine-day wine route](/multi-country/tour/chile-argentina-mendoza-wine-9-days/), Uco Valley lunch and an extra lunch at Concha y Toro have different terms. Compare each day and included/optional services without changing the pricing basis.

### Are there food tours without winery visits?

Yes. [Gastronomic Mexico](/mexico/tour/mexico-gourmet-discovery-2024/) focuses on local cooking, markets and regional dishes. On [Colombia coffee tours](/colombia/tour/colombia-coffee/), the main experience is growing, processing and brewing coffee. Wine is just one of the themes here.

### Can I add a food-focused day to an ordinary tour?

Sometimes. Separate excursions include [Mendoza winery tastings](/argentina/mendoza/mendoza-wineries-wine-tasting/) and [a coffee farm near Pereira](/colombia/pereira/pereira-coffee-farm-tour/). But their appearance on the website does not mean they are prepaid or fit any trip. First check the locations, free hours and transport.

### When should I visit Mendoza for wine?

For Vendimia, February–March are the broad guide; check specific events for the year. Normal winery tours need not fall during harvest. Choose your [wine itinerary](/multi-country/tour/chile-argentina-mendoza-wine-9-days/) first and then compare dates with the estate visits.

**Compare 2–3 journeys with the same main theme**, checking the real number of tastings and visits day by day. If you have not selected a culinary destination, begin with the [general food-and-wine guide](/interests/food-and-wine/); use this catalog to select available tours.

## Gastronomic tours in Mexico: which itinerary to choose

Our catalog contains {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}}. They differ mainly in time devoted to food. Markets, tacos and mezcal form a substantial independent part of one trip. A second folds a mezcal-production visit into a short Oaxaca stay. A third covers multiple regions, with local dishes adding to history and city sightseeing.

| Itinerary | Main theme |
|---|---|
| [9 days: food tour](/mexico/tour/mexico-gourmet-discovery-2024/) | Markets, tacos, mezcal |
| [5 days: Oaxaca](/mexico/tour/oaxaca-city-break-5-days/) | Mezcal and crafts |
| [12 days: “Viva Mexico”](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/) | Mexico City, Oaxaca, Yucatán |

**For a trip primarily devoted to Mexican food**, select the [nine-day food route](/mexico/tour/mexico-gourmet-discovery-2024/). If making agave spirits, craft workshops and staying in one city are your main interests, see the [five-day Oaxaca journey](/mexico/tour/oaxaca-city-break-5-days/). [“Viva Mexico”](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/) lets you experience several regional cuisines during a larger cultural trip.

## Mexico City: markets, street food and neighborhood flavors

The [nine-day food tour](/mexico/tour/mexico-gourmet-discovery-2024/) begins in the capital. It includes a gastronomic walk around [Coyoacán](/mexico/place/coyoacan/), taquerías and mezcal, and visits to San Juan and Medellín markets. Markets display ingredients rarely seen together on tourist menus: corn, various chilies, herbs, vegetables, spices and mole ingredients.

**Traditional Mexican cuisine was added to UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage list in 2010.** Corn, beans and chilies are central, while nixtamalization—treating maize kernels in an alkaline solution before making dough—is an important technique. On a food walk, ask not just the name of a dish but how local cooks prepare tortillas, sauces and fillings.

There is a distinct cultural component too. From Mexico City, the route goes to the [Xochimilco canals](/mexico/place/xochimilco/) and [Teotihuacán](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/), then continues on the Yucatán Peninsula. Stops include [Chichén Itzá](/mexico/place/chichen-itza/), [Cobá](/mexico/place/coba/) and [Tulum](/mexico/place/tulum/), with free days in [Cancún](/mexico/place/cancun/). You get food excursions alongside several days by the Caribbean.

**What is actually paid for:** the nine-day program covers daily breakfasts, lunch on the Chichén Itzá outing and tastings on food excursions. Other drinks, personal spending and the Mexico City–Cancún flight are extra. Restaurant visits in a program are not equivalent to all restaurant meals being prepaid.

## Oaxaca: discovering mezcal over 5 days

The [short Oaxaca trip](/mexico/tour/oaxaca-city-break-5-days/) focuses on one area while leaving time for town and nearby sites. It combines historic [Oaxaca](/mexico/place/oaxaca/), [Monte Albán](/mexico/place/monte-alban/), craft communities and [Mitla](/mexico/place/mitla/), exploring links between everyday traditions, art and regional products.

Day four includes a mezcal-production visit. Guests learn about agave cultivation and the stages of making the spirit, then taste it. That day also passes [Teotitlán del Valle](/mexico/place/teotitlan-del-valle/) and [Hierve el Agua](/mexico/place/hierve-el-agua/). For more detail, consult the standalone [Mitla, Hierve el Agua and mezcal tasting excursion](/mexico/mitla/mitla-hierve-el-agua-mescal-tour/).

The basic five-day package covers 4 nights with breakfast, 1 lunch, days 2–4 excursions and mezcal tasting. **Cooking workshops and extra tastings are excluded.** Airport transfers are private; the days 2–4 excursions are shared, with English- and Spanish-speaking guides. The exact day of the included lunch needs clarification because some individual excursion terms list food as an extra.

This is a good choice when exploring one area thoroughly matters more than switching cities every 1–2 days. A separate [Oaxaca city tour](/mexico/oaxaca/oaxaca-walking-tour/) focuses on the architecture. Its availability in the catalog does not mean every additional visit or restaurant is included in the package.

## Mexico City, Oaxaca and Yucatán: food on a broader journey

The [12-day “Viva Mexico”](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/) connects the capital, Oaxaca and Yucatán. Food complements a more extensive program of historic Mexico City districts, archaeological complexes, craft workshops, cenotes and peninsula towns.

In Oaxaca, a day in [Mitla](/mexico/place/mitla/) introduces mezcal traditions. Later in [Mérida](/mexico/place/merida/), visitors are advised to try cochinita pibil, sopa de lima and papadzules. The text offers restaurant recommendations; it does not describe a paid gastronomic excursion for that day.

The twelve-day route includes 11 nights' lodging with breakfasts and 1 lunch. Domestic and international flights are excluded. Check whether connections between Mexico City, Oaxaca and Mérida suit you. If tastings at several establishments every day are the main goal, the specialized [nine-day gastronomic tour](/mexico/tour/mexico-gourmet-discovery-2024/) is a better match.

## Mezcal, tequila and grape wine: what is included

Both mezcal and tequila come from agave, but they have different protected geographical designations and production rules. Tequila is made from blue agave in defined parts of five Mexican states, principally Jalisco. Mezcal can use different agave species; Oaxaca is a major traditional producing region.

**The experiences in these journeys specifically relate to mezcal.** The five-day Oaxaca tour includes production and tasting, the nine-day gastronomic tour includes a tasting during a walk, and the twelve-day route introduces the mezcal tradition. Each has its own format and amount of time.

For grape wine, Mexico has an important wine region in Valle de Guadalupe, Baja California. However, **none of these three programs lists winery visits there**. The “Food and Wine” title covers varied journeys; a listing in this category cannot guarantee a winery tour. Agree on a separate wine itinerary and tasting program if that is your purpose.

For journeys with confirmed winery visits, see the [Latin America food-and-wine tours catalog](/interests/food-and-wine/tours/). For geography and attractions, consult the [Mexico guide](/mexico/).

## Gastronomic tours in Nicaragua: where the culinary activities take place

## Granada and Masaya: discovering Nicaraguan cuisine

The Nicaragua segment particularly suits those who want to try local food in the everyday life of a city. On day 8, travelers explore [Granada](/nicaragua/place/granada/), take a boat on [Lake Nicaragua](/nicaragua/place/lake-nicaragua/) and stop at [Zopango Island](/nicaragua/place/zopango-island/). In Granada, try **vigorón**: boiled cassava, crispy pork cracklings and cabbage slaw with a sour dressing, traditionally served on a banana leaf. Nicaragua's tourism agency says it is sold near Granada's central park. Sampling it fits a stroll through the historic center, **if the full sightseeing schedule leaves time**.

The Masaya market mentioned in the itinerary is chiefly a **handicrafts market**. A visit does not imply a traditional-food tasting, a cooking activity or a separate culinary guide. Arrange such an experience separately.

## Foods worth trying in Nicaragua

Nicaraguan cuisine uses corn, rice, beans, cassava, plantains and local produce. Ingredients and cooking methods differ across Pacific, central and Caribbean regions. It helps to recognize these dishes before a trip through Granada and its surroundings.

| Dish or drink | Description |
|---|---|
| Vigorón | Cassava, pork cracklings, cabbage slaw |
| Gallo pinto | Rice and beans |
| Nacatamal | Filled corn dough cooked in leaves |
| Baho | Meat, cassava and plantains |
| Pinolillo | Drink made from corn and cacao |

**Gallo pinto** is eaten at breakfast and throughout Central American daily life, with serving styles varying by country and restaurant. **Nacatamal** is filled corn dough wrapped in leaves and steamed. **Baho** combines meat and root crops; **pinolillo** introduces corn and cacao together in a drink.

These are ideas for independent café and menu choices. **None is listed as a guaranteed meal on the 12-day tour.** Try them according to the time left after excursions and your food preferences.

## Gastronomic tours in Panama: what is really included

**The main gastronomic experience on these itineraries is discovering Geisha coffee in mountain [Boquete](/panama/place/boquete/).** One tour schedules a tasting after a canopy adventure; another includes a farm visit in a busy western Panama day; the third offers a shared English-language coffee tour. All include much more than coffee, visiting [Panama City](/panama/place/panama-city/), natural areas and seaside resorts.

Our catalog includes {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} with visits to Panama and a food-and-wine theme. Each discussed route takes place in Panama; food occupies one defined day or part of it. This matters to those seeking a multi-day culinary vacation: coffee accompanies the wider journey rather than replacing other activities. For farms, coffee varieties and bean processing, see [coffee journeys](/interests/coffee-tours/). For an overview of the country, read the [Panama guide](/panama/).

### How the three journeys differ

| [“Best of Panama,” 11 days](/panama/tour/best-of-panama-2023/) | Day 5: plantation and tasting after canopy |
| [“Luxury Panama,” 12 days](/panama/tour/luxury-panama-12-days/) | Day 7: shared English-language coffee tour |

## Choosing a trip for coffee and other experiences

### 11 days: tasting after a canopy adventure

The [11-day “Best of Panama” tour](/panama/tour/best-of-panama-2023/) begins with sightseeing in the capital and a visit to an Emberá community in [Chagres National Park](/panama/place/chagres-national-park/). It then moves to the Pacific coast and Chiriquí's mountains.

**On day 5**, travelers depart Boca Chica for Boquete. The morning starts with a canopy activity above the forest and river, followed **at 13:00 by a coffee plantation visit and tasting**, including Geisha. This option suits travelers who want one substantial encounter with coffee culture. The day is quite full: the published itinerary does not include a separate multi-hour barista course or several farm visits.

The next day is devoted to an off-road ascent of [Barú Volcano](/panama/place/baru-volcano/). Then the route continues to [Bocas del Toro](/panama/place/bocas-del-toro/) for relaxation and free time. If rainforest, ocean and good coffee appeal equally, this combines all three without a prolonged stay in the coffee region.

### 12 days: coffee farm and detailed accommodation arrangements

The [12-day luxury Panama tour](/panama/tour/luxury-panama-12-days/) covers the capital, [Gatún Lake](/panama/place/gatun-lake/), Chagres, Boca Chica, Boquete and the Caribbean. It has private-island leisure days, with accommodation and meals during that portion.

**On day 7**, the group travels from Boca Chica to Boquete and checks into the Panamonte Inn & Spa. The afternoon features a plantation associated with Geisha coffee. One key detail: **the coffee excursion is shared and conducted in English**. Remember this even if other days have private transfers or a guide. The published program does not promise a separate private Russian-speaking coffee guide.

There are gastronomic details outside the plantation: on the island, breakfast, lunch, snacks and a three-course dinner are listed, along with local beer, wines and cocktails. But these are **meals and drinks during a resort stay**, not winery visits or a dedicated wine-tasting itinerary. Check the exact inclusion and exclusion list on this tour's page rather than assuming it applies to other programs.

### 16 days: more regions, with coffee midway through a long journey

The [16-day Panama itinerary](/panama/tour/panama-2024/) allocates more time to historical and natural stops. After the [Panama Canal](/panama/place/panama-canal/) and Chagres, visitors travel to the San Blas Islands, see forts near [Portobelo](/panama/place/portobelo/), relax around Boca Chica, then reach Boquete and the Caribbean islands.

**Day 11** begins with a canopy tour, and **at 13:00** there is a coffee-plantation visit with a Geisha tasting. It does not offer separate days for multiple farms or an independent roasting course. Instead, the itinerary covers more of the country without rushing home after the western mountains.

This makes sense for travelers planning one comprehensive Panama holiday, combining coffee, [Barú Volcano](/panama/place/baru-volcano/), islands and history. For a coffee-only trip, compare transfer time with actual hours on the farm: the sixteen-day itinerary's chief advantage is the breadth of the country.

## Why Boquete became Panama's coffee center

[Boquete](/panama/place/boquete/) lies in the mountains of western Panama's Chiriquí Province. According to Panama's tourism authority, local coffee estates occupy elevations of approximately **1,000–2,100 m above sea level**. Volcanic soils, humidity, rainfall, terrain and a cooler climate than the lowland coasts shape cultivation.

The **Geisha** variety is internationally famous for the quality of some Panamanian lots. Compare tasting samples on more than the name: the farm, harvest, processing, roast and brewing all affect the result. Two Geisha cups may differ much more than a new taster expects.

Farms in the region explain how coffee trees are grown, berries harvested, beans processed and coffee brewed. But excursions differ by estate. **Ada Tours programs confirm plantation visits, not every detailed production stage a visitor personally gets to see.** Check those against the specific itinerary rather than a general list of regional possibilities.

Ask yourself: “Do I want to taste Geisha or understand how flavors vary?” One good tasting serves the first; for the second, pay more attention to fermentation, drying and roasting. Multiple producers require a longer coffee-focused stay than the single farm day on the three current routes.

## When to visit Panama for coffee

**Coffee excursions in Boquete run in different months**, but farm activities change with the agricultural cycle. Panama's tourism authority identifies **December–March** as the regional harvest period. Visitors may see ripe red berries and pickers at work if the particular farm opens that stage of production to guests.

Visits remain rewarding after harvest: farms offer explanations of processing, roasting and brewing. In **March–April**, coffee plants may flower in the mountains; during wetter months landscapes are particularly green. Flowering and harvest dates depend on elevation and weather, so no month guarantees either.

Panama generally has a drier season **from roughly December through April**, with wetter conditions during the rest of the year. Mountain Boquete is cooler, and mist or rain can occur even in the dry season. For [Barú Volcano](/panama/place/baru-volcano/) and canopy activities, bring warm layers and rain protection. Local organizers monitor mountain roads and the availability of activities.

To see **coffee harvesting**, aim for December–March and confirm the exact farm experience. For **tasting**, the suitable season is wider; the choice of farm and itinerary matters more than dates.

## What else to eat in Panama beyond Geisha

Panama's cuisine goes beyond coffee. [Panama City](/panama/place/panama-city/) blends traditional dishes with Caribbean and international influences. Fish, ceviche, fried plantains, corn-based foods and local products are all available. [Casco Viejo](/panama/place/casco-viejo/) is chiefly interesting for architecture and city atmosphere; nearby restaurants do not automatically make an ordinary sightseeing tour gastronomic.

Ada Tours has a confirmed example of local food: an Emberá community visit in [Chagres](/panama/place/chagres-national-park/) includes **a traditional lunch of fried tilapia, plantains and fruit**. This links food to local produce and daily life. But the excursion also covers crafts, traditions and a river trip; it is not a standalone cooking workshop.

Another agritourism theme around [Bocas del Toro](/panama/place/bocas-del-toro/) is **cacao**. Regional farms introduce guests to cacao cultivation and chocolate making, and Panama's tourism authority describes Indigenous communities participating in such experiences. **A cacao-farm visit is not advertised on any of the three Ada Tours tours described.** It is an idea for a separate tailored program if chocolate matters alongside coffee.

The same applies to wine. The website category is “Food and Wine,” but **plantation coffee is actually included while wineries and special wine tastings are not present on these three itineraries**. Travelers whose priority is wine should compare [other gastronomic tours](/interests/food-and-wine/tours/) in South America's wine regions.

## Fitting a coffee day into a Panama itinerary

Distances and terrain matter as much as theme. [Panama City](/panama/place/panama-city/) and western Boquete are on opposite sides of the country. These journeys use a flight to David and ground transfers, not a quick round trip to a farm from the capital. On the [11-day route](/panama/tour/best-of-panama-2023/), the drive from Boca Chica to Boquete takes about one and a half hours; the [12-day itinerary](/panama/tour/luxury-panama-12-days/) also includes this transfer.

Coffee visits often sit beside active pursuits. One itinerary starts the day with canopy; another visits [Barú Volcano](/panama/place/baru-volcano/) and mountain paths the next day. Western Panama's mountain roads and weather differ from the capital; cool and humid conditions mean that spare time is better kept as a real buffer than filled with extra mandatory activities.

Caribbean destinations include [Bocas del Toro](/panama/place/bocas-del-toro/), while Pacific beach time includes Boca Chica and islands in the Gulf of Chiriquí. This is attractive if you want to see different coastlines after a farm visit. But the sea and islands occupy much of the schedule: **a longer overall tour may simply have more days unrelated to coffee**.

Choose your main priority. For **a first introduction**, one tasting is enough. For **a broad cultural and seaside journey**, compare all stops. For **in-depth coffee study**, agree separately on desired farms, bean-processing methods and time in Boquete.
